entries.verbatim:
One of our beauty brands went from email/SMS contributing <10% of store revenue to 20% in about a month.

The biggest lever we pulled? Rebuilding the welcome popup.

Instead of the usual 'give us your email, get X% OFF' setup, we turned it into a full page takeover and gave customers two options: free shipping or a free gift.

The free gift was where it got interesting.

We didn’t tell them what it was on the popup. If they picked it, they had to open the welcome email to find out what they got.

That little bit of curiosity did a lot of work.

Popup submit rates went from 3% to 20%, and email/SMS contribution went from <10% to 20% in about a month.

And before someone asks about attribution, that’s measured on a 1-day click / 1-day open window.

As we ramp into Q4, popup acquisition and Welcome E1 are two of the biggest levers you can still pull.

By now, you should already have a pretty good idea of which offers are working.

If you don’t, start testing like mad now.

You don't want to be figuring that out in November.

entries.anchored_on:
A single Klaviyo number will not tell you how your retention is doing.

Here is the stack we actually read on an account:

- Klaviyo revenue as a percentage, next to Northbeam revenue as a percentage
- The Northbeam to Klaviyo revenue ratio, week over week and year over year
- Email revenue against SMS revenue
- Opens, clicks, unique opens, unique clicks, unsubs, spam and bounces, as percentages
- Emails sent against web sessions
- Click and revenue per recipient
- Percentage of checkout orders that include a subscription
- How many subscribers we touched with email and SMS in a 24 hour window, against baseline

We do not read all of this to report a number. We read it to know what to change next.
entries.verbatim:
If you’re using one Klaviyo number to tell you whether retention is healthy, you’re probably missing half the story.

We almost never look at Klaviyo in isolation.

If email is contributing 25% of revenue, cool.

But what happened to total Shopify revenue?

What does Northbeam say?

Has the Northbeam : Klaviyo revenue ratio moved WoW or YoY?

Did email grow because the channel got better, or because SMS fell off?

Did revenue per recipient improve, or did we just send more?

That’s how we actually read an account.

We’re looking at things like:

Shopify revenue, Klaviyo revenue %, Northbeam revenue %, and how those move against each other
Email vs SMS revenue, CTR and revenue per recipient
Opens, unique opens, clicks, unique clicks, unsubs, spam and bounces
Total emails sent against web sessions
Weekly, quarterly and YoY movement
% of checkout orders that include a subscription
How many subscribers got touched by email + SMS inside 24 hours, against baseline

None of those numbers are particularly interesting on their own.

It’s the relationship between them that tells you what’s going on.

Revenue can be up while efficiency is getting worse.

Klaviyo contribution can look great while the rest of the store is down.

You can send more, make more revenue, and still be quietly burning the list underneath it.

That’s why the question isn’t:

“What did Klaviyo report?”

It’s:

“What changed, relative to what, and what do we change next?”

entries.post: 5 (X) — If an agent violates a boundary…
entries.anchored_on:
engineers) - (Long-form)
I think this is an important distinction as agents get better at completing tasks:

AgentMail had a permission bug, and it lived in drafts.

An agent could be blocked from sending an email. It could still get one sent.

Creating a draft was allowed, but scheduling that draft didn’t check the send permission.

A minute later, a message the agent couldn’t send directly could go out through another path.

Our team fixed this by requiring send permission when a draft is scheduled on creation and on update. The mistake was treating “create a draft” as a harmless operation when one field turned it into a future send.
